section.title: Tola and Jair
section.sectionRationale: After the bloody self-destruction of Abimelech in chapter 9, the narrative breathes. Two judges, Tola and Jair, are given only a few quiet verses each: no battles are recorded, no speeches, only their tribe, their years, their sons, their towns, and their graves. These so-called minor judges show that God kept raising up deliverers for His people even in seasons without drama, and their calm brevity sets up, by contrast, the storm of Jephthah that follows.
section.thesis: Even after Abimelech's carnage, the LORD keeps providing deliverers for Israel, and the quiet, undramatic faithfulness of Tola and Jair testifies that God's care for His people runs on steadily through years that make no headlines.
section.frameNote: Two brief notices: Tola of Issachar who rose up to save Israel and judged twenty-three years, verses 1 to 2; and Jair the Gileadite with his thirty sons and thirty towns, who judged twenty-two years, verses 3 to 5.

units.label: Tola of Issachar
units.note: he rose up to save Israel

verses.text: After the time of Abimelech, a man of Issachar, Tola son of Puah, the son of Dodo, {{qum|rose up}} to {{yasha|save}} Israel. He lived in Shamir, in the hill country of Ephraim.
Tola {{shaphat|judged}} Israel twenty-three years, and when he died, he was buried in Shamir.
Tola was followed by Jair the Gileadite, who {{shaphat|judged}} Israel twenty-two years.
He had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys. And they had thirty towns in the land of Gilead, which to this day are called Havvoth-jair.
When Jair died, he was buried in Kamon.

qum.gloss: To rise up, arise, stand. Tola rose up to save Israel; the verb marks the moment God brings a deliverer onto the stage. Throughout Judges the raising up of a judge is God's own initiative, and the same word is later used of the prophet and the King God will raise up for His people.

yasha.gloss: To save, deliver, rescue. Tola rose up to save Israel. It is the root behind the name Joshua and Jesus, the LORD saves; even these brief, obscure judges are cast as saviors, small shadows of the great Deliverer to come.

shaphat.gloss: To judge, govern, lead, deliver justice. The book of Judges is named for the shophet, the judge, who was less a courtroom official than a Spirit-raised deliverer and leader. Tola and Jair each judged Israel for over twenty years, keeping order and rest between the crises.

basic.context: Chapter 9 ended in horror: Abimelech, Gideon's son, murdered his brothers and grasped at kingship until he and the men of Shechem destroyed one another. Now the pace slows right down. Two judges are named, Tola of Issachar and Jair of Gilead, and we are told almost nothing about them: their families, how long they led, and where they were buried. No wars, no words, no failures are recorded. These are usually called the minor judges, not because they mattered less, but because their stories are short. Their quiet notices show that God kept on providing leaders to hold Israel together even in years that produced no dramatic rescue.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative, and these verses are deliberately spare. We should not read too much into the silence, nor invent adventures the text does not give. The point lies in the pattern: after chaos, God raises up a deliverer; life settles for a generation; then the notice of a death and a burial closes the account. The repeated shape teaches that God's faithfulness is not measured only by spectacular deliverances but also by long, unremarkable stretches of steady leadership.
basic.originalLanguages: Tola qum, rose up, to yasha, save, Israel; the verb save is the root behind the names Joshua and Jesus, the LORD saves. Both men shaphat, judged, Israel, the very word that names the book, describing not a courtroom judge but a God-given deliverer and leader. Jair's thirty sons on thirty donkeys in thirty towns hint at wealth and influence, a settled, prosperous rule.
basic.typology: Every judge who rises up to save is a small, flawed picture of the true Savior. Tola, whose very role is to save Israel, faintly foreshadows the one whose name means the LORD saves, Jesus, who rises up not for a generation but forever. The quiet rest these judges secured points ahead to the lasting rest Christ gives His people.
basic.christ: These minor judges are cast as saviors of Israel, and the word for save is the root of the name Jesus. Where Tola and Jair rose up for a time and then were buried, Christ rose up to save, died, and rose again never to be buried, an unending Deliverer. Their brief, God-given leadership points to the King the whole book longs for, the righteous Savior who reigns forever.
basic.god: God is the quiet, faithful provider behind these bare verses. He is the one who raises up deliverers, even ones whose deeds are never recorded, so that His people are never left without care. He works not only in the headline rescues but through years of ordinary, steady leadership, showing a patient, providential kindness that keeps His people even when nothing dramatic is happening.
basic.crossReferences: Judges 2 gives the framework in which the LORD raised up judges to deliver His people. Acts 13 lists the judges in the story of God's dealings with Israel. And Hebrews 11 gathers many such deliverers, some barely named, as witnesses of faith, reminding us that God honors the obscure as well as the famous.
basic.oneStory: After Abimelech's ruin, God quietly raises up Tola and Jair to keep His people. Their brief, faithful years are one more link in the long chain of deliverers God provides, a chain that runs through all the judges and points beyond them to the one Savior who rises up to save and reigns forever.

context.literary:
These five verses are the shortest unit in the entire book, yet their placement does real literary work. They form a deliberate pause between two of the longest and most violent narratives Judges contains, Abimelech's three years of bloodshed just concluded and Jephthah's tragic vow and civil war about to begin, so their calm is not incidental but constructed, a breath the narrator inserts before plunging back into crisis. Both notices share an identical minimal formula, name, patronym or origin, a verb of leading, years served, one distinguishing detail, and a burial notice, a template scholars call the minor judge formula because it recurs with only small variation for Shamgar, Tola, Jair, Ibzan, Elon and Abdon scattered across the book.

The formula's very sparseness is the point: unlike the judges given long narrative treatment, these men generate no plot, no crisis, no moral commentary, because nothing about their tenures produced one. Read against the surrounding chapters, the two notices function almost like a ledger entry confirming that the years did not go unaccounted for even when they produced no memorable events, and their combined forty five years, twenty three for Tola and twenty two for Jair, quietly cover nearly two generations of otherwise undocumented national life, holding the larger cycle of sin and deliverance in suspension for longer than almost any single crisis narrative in the book.
context.historical:
Tola's home, Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim, is otherwise unattested in Scripture and cannot be securely located, though its placement in Ephraim, rather than in Issachar, his own tribe, suggests a leader whose authority crossed ordinary tribal lines, much as Deborah, also based in Ephraim's hill country, had judged before him. Jair operated on the opposite side of the Jordan, in Gilead, a region of scattered fortified towns rather than one great city, well suited to a network of loosely allied settlements each under a local strongman's kin.

His thirty sons riding thirty donkeys, rather than horses or mules, signals status appropriate to a settled, prosperous clan rather than a war leader, since donkeys were a standard mount of peacetime nobility throughout the region. That this Jair shares his name exactly with an earlier Manassite commander who had already captured and named a cluster of villages Havvoth-jair generations before, in the days of the conquest, Numbers 32:41 and Deuteronomy 3:14, means either that the judge descended from and reasserted a family claim to ancestral territory, or that two men centuries apart happened to share a name attached to the same region, a coincidence Gilead's own genealogies would have made unremarkable.
context.canonical:
Two later summaries of Israel's history treat men like Tola and Jair as fully continuous with the more famous judges rather than as a lesser category. Paul, preaching at Pisidian Antioch, simply says that God gave them judges until Samuel the prophet, about four hundred and fifty years, Acts 13:20, folding twelve very different careers, dramatic and undramatic alike, into a single, unbroken account of divine provision. The writer to the Hebrews goes further still, placing Gideon in the same short list of examples as prophets and kings, Hebrews 11:32, implying that faith, not fame, is the quality Scripture actually cares to commend, a standard by which Tola and Jair, however briefly described, qualify exactly as fully as Gideon or Samson.

Their brevity also anticipates a recurring biblical pattern in which faithful, ordinary service goes almost unrecorded compared to crisis leadership, the same pattern that will later let a book like Ruth spend four chapters on a single obscure family while a king's whole reign receives a single verse of genealogy. And their era falls precisely inside the long interval the book of Judges keeps measuring against its own refrain, that in those days Israel had no king, Judges 21:25, a gap this quiet stretch fills without yet resolving.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: Placed exactly where they are, these five verses teach the first hearers something Abimelech's chapter alone could not teach them, that God's provision for His people does not depend on drama to be real. A reader who has just watched a self-made king burn a city and die by a millstone could easily conclude that all leadership after judges of God's own choosing collapses into chaos; Tola and Jair interrupt that conclusion before it can harden, showing that ordinary, sustained, unspectacular governance was still available and was still God's gift even in the very same turbulent period. The author's intent is corrective as much as informative: Israel, and every later reader tempted to measure God's faithfulness only by the size of the miracle attached to it, needs reminding that twenty three quiet years of order are just as much evidence of divine care as one dramatic night of trumpets and torches.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The text simply records who led, for how long, and where they were buried; it prescribes no leadership model, no minimum length of service, and no specific virtue beyond what the bare fact of stability implies. Readers should resist manufacturing a hidden lesson from Jair's thirty sons and thirty towns as though large families or landholding were themselves marks of spiritual success, since the text offers these details as simple historical notice rather than commendation or warning, unlike the pointed criticism attached to Gideon's ephod just one chapter earlier. What legitimately carries forward is the pattern beneath the details: God's ordinary provision of order and rest, sustained across long, undramatic stretches, deserves the same gratitude as His extraordinary deliverances, even though only the latter tend to be remembered or celebrated.

debates.question: Why does Scripture give the minor judges such short, undramatic notices?

views.label: They led in relatively peaceful times
views.case: The absence of recorded wars may mean their years were genuinely calmer, so the text simply notes their steady leadership without a crisis to narrate; the brevity reflects the quiet of the era, not a lesser importance.

views.label: The author is being selective for a purpose
views.case: Judges is shaped around the downward spiral of the nation, so the writer lingers on the accounts that make that point and compresses others; the minor judges are noted to show the continuity of God's provision while the spotlight stays on the larger theme.

debates.bearing: Either way, the brief notices affirm that God kept providing deliverers, and they teach us to value faithful, obscure service as well as the famous rescues.

debates.question: Is Judges' Jair the same man remembered generations earlier in Numbers 32:41, or a later namesake?

views.label: A revived ancestral claim
views.case: Numbers 32:41 and Deuteronomy 3:14 already record a Manassite named Jair capturing and naming these same villages, Havvoth-jair, centuries earlier, in the days of Moses. On this view the judge either descends from that ancestor and reasserts a family holding, or the text simply intends readers to recognize a family name still attached, generations on, to the very land it first named.

views.label: A separate man who shares a common family name
views.case: Given how many generations separate the conquest era from the judges, and how common such family names could be within a single clan settled in one region, the repetition may be no more than coincidence of naming rather than any claimed continuity, the judge simply belonging to the same wider Gileadite line without any implied restoration of a specific ancestor's exploits.

debates.bearing: Either way, the two accounts together show that a single life could leave its mark most durably not through the deeds recorded about it but through a place name that outlived the deeds by many centuries, exactly the kind of quiet, non-dramatic legacy this whole passage is built to honor.

study.originalLanguages:
Tola's genealogy is unusually full for so brief a notice, son of Puah, the son of Dodo, three generations named where most of the minor judges receive only a single patronym or none at all. The same two names surface elsewhere in very different settings, Puah as one of the two Hebrew midwives who defied Pharaoh, Exodus 1:15, and Dodo as the father of one of David's mighty men, Elhanan son of Dodo, 2 Samuel 23:24. Nothing ties these bearers of the names to Tola's own family; the coincidence simply shows how a small, stable stock of family names recurred across tribes and centuries in ancient Israel, the kind of detail a genealogically minded people would have noticed and a modern reader easily misses.

Qum, rise up, deserves one further observation beyond its use for Tola. The same verb describes Deborah rising as a mother in Israel, Judges 5:7, and later becomes part of the standard vocabulary for a prophet raised up by God, as when the LORD promises Moses that He will raise up a prophet like him from among the people, Deuteronomy 18:15. The verb therefore belongs to a specific biblical pattern of divine commissioning; whenever someone rises to lead or to save in the Old Testament, the text is quietly claiming that the initiative and the timing both belong to God rather than to human ambition or opportunity.

Shaphat, judge, likewise carries more freight than the English word suggests. It never describes, in this book, a robed official presiding over a courtroom; it describes someone who restores right order to a whole community, the broad, restorative sense of setting crooked things straight rather than the narrow sense of issuing verdicts. Reading Tola and Jair as men who restored justice to Israel for over twenty years each, rather than as mere administrators, brings their bare notices closer to what the word itself was actually claiming about their work.

Even the place names carry quiet theology. Shamir, Tola's town, and Kamon, where Jair is buried, along with Havvoth-jair, the region his sons controlled, all simply preserve a family's memory in the land long after any record of their deeds survives, exactly the kind of afterlife these two verses are content to grant their subjects.

typology.type: Tola, whose very name and role is bound up with saving Israel
typology.fulfillment: The verb that describes Tola rising up to save Israel, yasha, is the identical root later carried by the name given to Mary's son, you are to call His name Jesus, for He will save His people from their sins, Matthew 1:21. Every minor judge who rises up to save for a few decades and then is buried anticipates, without ever announcing it, the one final rising up to save that will not end in a grave, since this Savior did not stay dead, Acts 2:24.

typology.type: Jair's thirty sons riding in peace across a settled, undisputed Gilead
typology.fulfillment: The picture of an extended household moving freely on donkeys through towns that bear the family name is a small, local image of the wholeness and rest God's provision of a judge could produce for a generation. Isaiah later pictures the Messiah's reign in exactly this key, a king who will judge the poor with righteousness so that the wolf will dwell with the lamb, Isaiah 11:3-6, a peace Jair's Gilead enjoyed only briefly and only in miniature, but that Christ's kingdom will finally make permanent and complete.

typology.type: A deliverer buried and then, within a generation, all but forgotten by name
typology.fulfillment: Tola and Jair each receive a burial notice and nothing more, their memory kept alive only by a village name and a scattered genealogical note. Christ's burial, by contrast, becomes the very center of the gospel rather than its footnote, He was buried, and He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, 1 Corinthians 15:4, so that the one burial in Scripture that actually matters for salvation is the one burial no stone tomb could make permanent.

study.christ:
It would be easy to treat five verses about two obscure judges as having little to say about Christ at all, yet the very obscurity is itself part of what these verses preach. Scripture's confidence that God was still actively saving and governing His people through forty five quiet years, years without a single recorded miracle, battle or crisis, teaches exactly the patience the New Testament asks believers to have about a King who has likewise been reigning, unseen by the world's notice, since His ascension, until He appears again, Hebrews 10:12-13.

Tola's role, described with the same Hebrew root that will one day name Jesus, is a small but real down payment on the truth that salvation in the Bible is always personal before it is doctrinal, always carried out through someone rising up on behalf of others rather than delivered as an abstract principle. Every minor judge, precisely because his story is so thin, throws the reader's attention away from the deliverer's own qualities, which the text does not bother to describe, and onto the fact of deliverance itself, that God provided someone, which is finally what matters most about every judge in this book and supremely about Christ.

Jair's thirty sons, thirty donkeys and thirty towns, whatever else they signal about wealth and standing, describe a household enjoying peace and multiplication in the very same land that, one chapter later, will be plunged into an emergency Jephthah must be recruited to solve, Judges 10:6-9. The fragility of that peace, real while it lasted, unable to outlast Jair's own lifetime, is precisely the fragility every purely human peace carries. Christ's kingdom is the one peace the New Testament promises will not require a fresh judge every generation to renew it, since of the increase of His government and of peace there will be no end, Isaiah 9:7, a promise these quiet, temporary decades of rest can only gesture toward and never themselves fulfill.
study.god:
These verses show a God who counts the unremarkable years as carefully as the remarkable ones. Nothing about Tola's twenty three years or Jair's twenty two produced a single line worth narrating in detail, yet both spans are recorded with exact precision, named leader, named years, named burial place, as if heaven itself keeps a ledger that values faithful duration even when human history books would have nothing to say about it. This is a God who does not measure His own care for His people by the excitement level of the record it leaves behind.

He is also a God who provides continuously rather than sporadically. The text gives no indication of a gap between Abimelech's death and Tola's rising, or between Tola's death and Jair's, an unbroken sequence that quietly insists Israel was never for one day without some form of God-given leadership in this stretch of its history, however imperfect that leadership, and however little Scripture chooses to say about it. The same God who thundered at Sinai and split a sea at the exodus is, in these verses, simply and steadily keeping a nation functioning for two generations running, and Scripture treats both kinds of action as equally His.

Finally, this passage reveals a God untroubled by being upstaged in the historical record. Human authors, ancient and modern alike, gravitate toward crisis and drama; God's own inspired record here refuses that gravitational pull, giving as much ink, relatively, to quiet governance as to spectacular deliverance, because His own priorities do not match a storyteller's instinct for drama. A God willing to let two of His servants be remembered in five verses, while still counting their combined forty five years as real and valuable service, is a God whose approval was never for sale to whoever could make the most exciting story out of it. Faithful obscurity, in His eyes, is never wasted time.

crossReferences.note: Puah is also the name of one of the two Hebrew midwives who defied Pharaoh's order to kill Israelite infant boys. Nothing connects the two directly, but the shared name shows how a small stock of names recurred across Israel's tribes and centuries, the same ordinary continuity these two minor judges themselves represent.

Dodo is also the name of the father of Elhanan, one of David's mighty men centuries later. As with Puah, there is no direct family link, only the quiet reminder that Scripture's genealogies preserve far more ordinary names than famous ones, exactly the kind of record Tola's own brief notice belongs to.

Deborah's song remembers that she herself rose, using the same verb of divine initiative that describes Tola rising up to save Israel. The two accounts, one sung in triumph and one recorded in a single flat sentence, both credit the same kind of God-given rising for very different scales of deliverance.

Moses promises that the LORD will one day raise up a prophet like himself from among the people. The same pattern of God raising up a needed leader, seen here in miniature through Tola, ultimately reaches its complete fulfillment in the prophet greater than Moses whom the New Testament identifies as Christ.

An earlier Manassite named Jair had already captured villages in Gilead centuries before and called them Havvoth-jair. Whether the judge of this chapter renewed an ancestral claim or simply shared a family name, the same place name binds the conquest generation to this later, quieter era of settled leadership.

Ibzan and Abdon, judges named just a few verses after Jephthah's crisis, are given an almost identical formula to Jair, sons, marriages or grandsons, donkeys and years served. The repetition across several separate minor judges shows this pattern of brief, formulaic notice was a deliberate literary convention, not a one time exception.

Isaiah promises a kingdom whose increase and peace will never end, ruled from David's throne forever. Jair's peaceful, prosperous household in Gilead offers only a brief, mortal preview of the endless increase and unbroken peace Isaiah credits to the far greater King still to come.

Paul states that Christ was buried and was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures. Tola and Jair are each simply buried, their story ending exactly where every human deliverer's story must end, making the one burial in Scripture that did not stay final all the more remarkable by contrast.

Faith, the writer says, is confidence in what is hoped for and certainty about what is not seen. Two judges remembered only by name, years and burial place ask readers to trust that God was genuinely at work across decades that produced no visible drama, exactly the kind of faith this verse describes.

study.oneStory:
Every chapter of Judges is building toward the same unresolved ache, and these five verses supply an unusual kind of evidence for that ache precisely because they contain no crisis at all. Between Abimelech's fire and Jephthah's coming vow, God simply keeps the nation functioning through two long, undramatic reigns, demonstrating that the deep problem Judges is diagnosing was never a shortage of competent, God-given leadership. Tola and Jair prove that ordinary provision was available in abundance; what the book's larger argument keeps proving is that even good, undramatic leadership cannot, by itself, change a people's underlying appetite to abandon the LORD the moment convenience allows.

This little pause also belongs to a much older pattern in the Bible's story, since the years just before great crises are often the quietest, the long silent stretch between Malachi and the birth of Christ, the decades of ordinary life in Nazareth before a single public miracle, entire generations of exile in Babylon that produced no prophet at all for long stretches. Scripture treats silence and slow time as no less a part of God's story than the loud interventions, since faith, as the New Testament will later put it, is confidence in what is not seen quite as much as gratitude for what has already been shown, Hebrews 11:1.

The rest of the Bible resolves what Tola and Jair could only hold in place for a while. Their combined forty five years bought Israel time it did not know how to use well, since Jephthah's crisis erupts the moment their notices end; but the same patient provision that raised them up is the provision that, many centuries and many disappointing judges and kings later, finally raises up a Savior whose reign will not need a successor, closing the very gap these quiet verses could only manage rather than heal.

quiz.q: What is said about Tola's role in Israel?

options.text: He rose up to save Israel and judged them twenty-three years.
options.note: Verses 1-2 describe Tola rising up to save and judging Israel for twenty-three years.

options.text: He judged Israel for many years in the hill country of Ephraim.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but it omits the key note that he rose up to save Israel.

options.text: He led Israel to a great victory in battle over Ammon.
options.note: No battle is recorded for Tola; that crisis comes later with Jephthah.

options.text: He seized power by force like Abimelech before him.
options.note: The opposite: Tola rose up to save Israel, unlike Abimelech who grasped at kingship.

quiz.q: What details are given about Jair the Gileadite?

options.text: He had thirty sons who rode thirty donkeys and held thirty towns, and he judged Israel twenty-two years.
options.note: Verses 3-4 record his sons, donkeys, towns, and years, signs of wealth and influence.

options.text: He was a prosperous leader in Gilead with a large family.
options.note: True in substance, but it leaves out the specific detail of his years and towns.

options.text: He built the city of Shamir and ruled from there.
options.note: Shamir was linked to Tola; Jair was buried in Kamon, and his towns were Havvoth-jair.

options.text: He refused to lead Israel and fled from his calling.
options.note: Nothing of the sort; Jair judged Israel for twenty-two years.

quiz.q: Why are Tola and Jair often called minor judges?

options.text: Because their accounts are brief, giving little more than their years, families, and burials.
options.note: The label reflects the short notices, not any lesser importance in God's provision.

options.text: Because they judged for only a very short time.
options.note: Misleading, since both judged for over twenty years; the brevity is in the text, not their tenure.

options.text: Because they were unfaithful and failed as leaders.
options.note: No failure is recorded; the notices are simply short, not critical.

options.text: Because they were never truly appointed by God.
options.note: Tola rose up to save Israel, and both are counted among the judges God provided.

quiz.q: What do these quiet notices teach about God?

options.text: That God keeps providing deliverers for His people even in undramatic times.
options.note: The pattern shows God's steady, faithful provision across ordinary years, not only crises.

options.text: That God cares only about the famous, dramatic rescues.
options.note: The reverse: these brief notices show God's care in quiet seasons too.

options.text: That God had abandoned Israel after Abimelech.
options.note: Far from abandonment, God raised up new deliverers right after the ruin of chapter 9.

options.text: That leaders no longer mattered to Israel's life.
options.note: The judges held Israel together; their leadership plainly mattered.

quiz.q: How does Tola's role point forward to Christ?

options.text: He rose up to save Israel, and the word for save is the root of the name Jesus, the LORD saves.
options.note: Tola is a small, temporary savior pointing to the great and final Savior, Jesus.

options.text: He rescued Israel from all their enemies forever.
options.note: His saving was real but temporary; only Christ saves finally and forever.

options.text: He was a sinless king who reigned without end.
options.note: Tola was a judge who died and was buried, not a sinless, eternal king; that is Christ alone.

options.text: He has no connection to the coming Savior.
options.note: His very role, to save Israel, foreshadows the Savior whose name means the LORD saves.

questions: Tola and Jair are barely described, yet God used them to keep His people. How does that comfort you if your own service feels obscure and unnoticed?
These judges rose up right after the chaos of Abimelech. Where have you seen God quietly provide steady leadership after a season of upheaval?
The text values long, unremarkable years of faithfulness as much as dramatic rescues. Are you tempted to think only the big, visible things count with God?
Tola rose up to save Israel, a faint shadow of Jesus, the LORD saves. How does knowing Christ is the true and lasting Savior steady you when human leaders come and go?
God never left His people without a deliverer. How can that assurance shape the way you trust Him in the ordinary stretches of your life right now?

translationNotes.note: Rose up to save translates a phrase that casts Tola as a deliverer; the verb for save, yasha, is the root behind the names Joshua and Jesus, the LORD saves.
Judged renders shaphat; the BSB footnote notes it can also mean governed or led, describing a God-given leader and deliverer rather than only a courtroom judge, here and throughout the book.
Havvoth-jair means the villages, or tent-camps, of Jair; the BSB footnote gives the villages of Jair, a place name that preserved his memory in Gilead.
